title: sampling-noise-quant-artifact-drift-jun2025
content:
Summary:

This is a working write-up of a set of microbenchmarks and qualitative checks we ran to investigate an intermittent output-drift / token-flakiness class of incidents that correlate with low-precision kernels (INT8/AWQ/GPTQ/FP8). The hypothesis is that quantization changes the token probability tail shape and interacts with non-deterministic sampler paths plus caching to produce reproducible-seeming but incorrect distributional shifts. This doc focuses on observed phenomena, a lightweight test harness, measured metrics, a few case studies, and immediate mitigations.

Goals:
- Identify metrics that capture sampling instability caused by quantized kernels (beyond BLEU/perplexity).
- Compare GPTQ, AWQ, INT8, and FP8 variants on a mix of deterministic and stochastic decoding.
- Isolate whether drift is due to kernel numerical noise, KV-cache wiring, or sampling nondeterminism.
- Produce short actionable mitigations to ship as part of Canary and SLA playbooks.

Test environment and assets:
- Hardware: a single A100-80GB and a V100 (for cross-arch differences).
- Runtime: serving-runtime main @ commit 7c3f2a (kernel-selector opt), with kernel build flavors: fast-kernel-v2, stable-kernel-v1.
- Models: LLaMA-2-13B (fp16 baseline), LLaMA-2-13B-GPTQ (4/16 split), LLaMA-2-13B-AWQ, LLaMA-2-13B-INT8 static, and an FP8 experimental build.
- Workloads: 1) temperature sampling set (nucleus p=0.9, temp 0.8) on 300 prompts (diverse style: instructions, code, dialogue). 2) greedy / beam deterministic set for 200 prompts to check deterministic drift. 3) long-prefix churn set (2k token prefixes + 512 token continuation) to stress KV-cache.
- Clients: replay harness with fixed RNG seeding option and an unconstrained replay. Each run captured per-token logits, sampled token, top-k probability vector (k=32), and kernel metadata (kernel id and build).

Key custom metrics we used:
- Token Flakiness Rate (TFR): fraction of prompt+prefix positions where sampled token differs between baseline FP16 run and quant run when RNG seed held constant. Computed across n prompts.
- Top-1 KL Spike Count: count of tokens where KL(logits_fp16 || logits_quant) > 1.2 nats (heuristic).
- Tail-Entropy Shift (TES): delta in Shannon entropy computed on top-32 distribution between baseline and quant.
- Deterministic Divergence Index (DDI): for deterministic decoding (greedy/beam), fraction of prompts whose final output string differs vs baseline.
- Latency / p50-p95 per-token observed on each kernel.

Findings (high-level):
1) Sampling-sensitive workloads (temp>0.6, nucleus sampling) show much higher TFR for AWQ and INT8 compared to GPTQ and FP8. Typical TFR observed: AWQ ~ 12-18%, INT8 static ~ 9-14%, GPTQ ~ 4-7%, FP8 ~ 3-5% (compared to fp16 baseline).
2) DDI is low for short prompts (<128 tokens) but grows on long-prefix churn tests, particularly when the runtime uses cached KV pages produced by quant kernels and then serves with a different kernel on continuation. We observed deterministic divergence up to 6% when kernel switchover occurred between prefix and continuation.
3) Top-1 KL spikes are concentrated at the token positions immediately after a sampling decision (i.e., after a high-entropy token). These spikes are larger for AWQ; TES correlates with TFR with Pearson r~0.68 in our samples.
4) Numerical noise in kernels (stochastic rounding in some AWQ implementations) amplifies randomness from top-k truncation. Enabling full 32-bit accumulation for attention reduce KL spikes by ~30% but costs ~8-12% latency.
5) Kernel scheduling jitter (switching to a high-throughput kernel mid-request for better latency) is a major practical source of divergence. When the runtime forces kernel pinning (same kernel for a full request), DDI dropped by ~75% on long-prefix tests.

Representative numbers (median of 5 runs; FP16 baseline normalized = 1.0):
- AWQ: per-token latency 0.72x, p95 latency 0.85x, TFR 0.15, DDI (long-prefix) 0.06, avg TES +0.42 bits
- GPTQ: per-token latency 0.78x, p95 latency 0.9x, TFR 0.055, DDI 0.015, avg TES +0.14 bits
- INT8 static: per-token latency 0.68x, p95 latency 0.88x, TFR 0.11, DDI 0.03, avg TES +0.3 bits
- FP8: per-token latency 0.85x, p95 latency 0.95x, TFR 0.04, DDI 0.01, avg TES +0.12 bits

Micro-investigations and notes:
- Seeded-replay experiment: we held PRNG seeds fixed at client and server. For AWQ runs on fast-kernel-v2 we still saw non-zero TFR. Exported per-token logits from both runs showed tiny perturbations around decision boundary which were enough to flip sampling. This indicates kernel numerical variation, not just RNG differences.
- Kernel build flags: enabling deterministic matmul paths (disable fused stochastic rounding) in AWQ nearly eliminated the seeded TFR but produced higher p95 latency. Tradeoff is latency vs deterministic quality.
- KV-cache wiring check: a bug was uncovered where cached KV blocks produced by an AWQ kernel used a different quant scale table when reloaded by the stable-kernel-v1 path. That produced catastrophic DDI in a small subset (~0.4%) of prompts. Patch PR #812 fixes the scale table sealing.
- Beam vs greedy: deterministic divergence occurs more in beam when quant logits compress inter-beam score margins. For beam width 5, GPTQ reduces inter-beam reorder probability by ~2x compared to AWQ.

Actionable mitigations (short-term):
1) Kernel pinning option: add route-level config to pin kernel variant for the full lifetime of a request (prefix + continuation). Default: pinned for requests > 512 tokens or when sampling is enabled. (Canary flag: kernel_pin=true).
2) Deterministic AWQ build for canary: provide a determinism-focused packaging of AWQ kernels (no stochastic rounding) to customers needing strict reproducibility. Trade: ~10% latency cost.
3) Sampling-aware regression checks: include TFR and TES as signals in our CI bench for each quantized model update. Thresholds: TFR <= 0.05 for production; TES <= 0.25 bits.
4) KV-cache sealing: ensure quant scale metadata is stored with KV blocks and validated on reload (fixed in PR #812).
5) Recommend customers doing high-consistency generation (e.g., code assistants) prefer GPTQ/FP8 if available; AWQ/INT8 provide cost wins but need stricter pinning.

Longer-term research directions:
- Explore hybrid decoding: run top-5 decoding in higher precision while keeping bulk matmuls quantized, to reduce tail sensitivity at modest cost.
- Profile per-layer sensitivity to sampling noise and design per-layer mixed-precision profiles (example: attention + early layers in fp16).
- Formalize a per-customer TFR budget exposed in Console (so customers can trade cost vs stability).

Open questions / TODOs:
- Re-run full suite across Mistral-7B and Llama-3 variants (pending model packaging).
- Quantify human-perceptible change rate on downstream tasks (e.g., code correctness, instruction following).
- Add a p95/p99 per-quant-run KL delta alarm into Console to catch regressions in production.

Appendix: quick reproduction steps
1) checkout serving-runtime@7c3f2a, build fast-kernel-v2 and stable-kernel-v1.
2) start local runtime with env RUNNER_DETERMINISM=off and RUNNER_KERN_PIN=false.
3) run harness: tools/quant-sampling-scan --prompts samples/seeded-300.json --model llm2-13b-awq --runs 5 --capture-logits --seed 1234
4) toggle RUNNER_DETERMINISM=on and repeat to compare.

Notes for PR/Canary: attach deterministic-AWQ binary as artifact and enable kernel_pin by default for canary routes that have sampling turned on.

If you want raw CSV/ndjson dumps from our runs, tell me which model + kernel + prompt subset and I'll upload to the bench S3 (we already have 5GB of captured logs for the experiment described).

Contributors: Leah (owner), Marcus (profiling harness, latency numbers), Priya (sampling analysis and KL tooling), Owen (kernel triage and PR #812).

End of note.
